screening: All 151 active identities screened and all plausible language, rhetoric, literature, history, media, art/heritage, sociology, politics, law, welfare and research content considered. Keywords are leads only; the 48-course ledger records substantive contributions and limits. No absent enrichment is reconstructed; description-only psycholinguistics, historiography, literary meaning, current American Century research, policy and social movements receive full weight.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.finding: Mandatory first-year academic writing, source evaluation, reflective inquiry and civic collaboration.

BENECON111.name: Introduction to Economics
BENECON111.finding: Economic models of markets and policy supply foundations for the trial’s public-economics analysis; not a Nordic economy course.

BENECON311.name: Public Economics
BENECON311.finding: Welfare, health, education, insurance, taxation and redistribution provide a substantive social-model bridge, without a documented Nordic comparative welfare sequence.

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.finding: Empirical design, surveys, measurement, inference and a full data-collection project supply social-research methods; no Nordic field setting is prescribed.

GOSGATE102.name: Law, Society & Justice
GOSGATE102.finding: Socio-legal analysis of institutions, rights, justice and social control supplies a complementary institutional method; not Scandinavian legal study.

GOSHIST111.name: Modern History
GOSHIST111.finding: Industrialisation, nationalism, migration, decolonisation and global modernity support historical comparison; no sustained Scandinavian regional narrative is established.

GOSHIST112.name: Histories of Gender
GOSHIST112.finding: Gender, family, sexuality, memory, interviews and cultural representation provide concrete historical methods and themes; the documented setting is North America.

GOSHIST211.name: History of Empires
GOSHIST211.finding: Comparative imperial power, ideology, administration and cultural legacies support historical explanation; specific Nordic colonial histories are not established.

GOSHIST311.name: Native American Histories
GOSHIST311.finding: Indigenous histories, institutional violence, resurgence and relational collaboration provide a real methodological connection to Indigenous cultural inquiry; Native American teaching is not Sami/Inuit regional instruction.

GOSHIST312.name: Researching the “American Century”
GOSHIST312.finding: The current official description supports historical questions, source criticism, interdisciplinary methods and a substantial paper. Its American title and bounded content do not establish Nordic research. The excluded historical outline is not used.

GOSLAWJ111.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
GOSLAWJ111.finding: Rights institutions and philosophical claims support questions of minorities, identity and recognition; not specifically Nordic rights history.

GOSLAWJ212.name: Introduction to Public International Law
GOSLAWJ212.finding: International law, self-determination, rights, institutions and postcolonial perspectives support cross-border and colonial comparison; not an Arctic legal sequence.

GOSLAWJ213.name: Comparative Constitutional Law
GOSLAWJ213.finding: Comparative constitutional institutions, rights and case interpretation offer concrete tools for political comparison, without establishing Scandinavian institutional study.

GOSLAWJ312.name: Foundations of European Union Law
GOSLAWJ312.finding: EU institutions, citizenship, free movement and casework provide relevant European connections, without a Nordic institutional/cultural focus.

GOSPHIL212.name: Ethics
GOSPHIL212.finding: Ethical theories and independent normative argument illuminate values, practices and meaning; not the region’s intellectual history.

GOSPHIL311.name: Philosophy of Emotion
GOSPHIL311.finding: Theories of emotion, art, politics and lived experience provide concepts for cultural interpretation; no Nordic case sequence is specified.

GOSPOLI111.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
GOSPOLI111.finding: Political authority, rights and ideological traditions support analysis of social models; no sustained Nordic intellectual or political history is established.

GOSPOLI112.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
GOSPOLI112.finding: Empirical comparison of democracy, institutions, participation and polarisation supports political inquiry. The old brief-Sweden claim is not corroborated by current profile/description and is not reused as regional content.

GOSPOLI212.name: Theory of International Relations
GOSPOLI212.finding: IR theories, cases and a researched UN simulation offer international institutional inquiry; a possible Nordic country choice cannot establish taught regional depth.

GOSPOLI311.name: European Union Politics
GOSPOLI311.finding: EU institutions, integration and an empirical parliamentary-amendment project offer substantive European political methods; not a Scandinavian politics sequence.

GOSPOLI312.name: Public Policy Analysis
GOSPOLI312.finding: The description supports globalisation, policy processes, a sugar case and policy memos; this receives full weight without inventing Nordic policy cases.

GOSPOLI313.name: Peace & Conflict
GOSPOLI313.finding: Conflict, colonial legacies, identity, rights and peacebuilding provide interdisciplinary comparison, not documented Baltic/Arctic regional study.

GOSSOCI111.name: Introduction to Sociology
GOSSOCI111.finding: Solidarity, modernity, identity, inequality and social boundaries supply direct social concepts, with general applications rather than a Scandinavian survey.

GOSSOCI212.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
GOSSOCI212.finding: Interviews, observation, ethnography, coding and reflexive research support regional-study methods; a freely chosen Nordic project is not guaranteed instruction or supervision.

GOSSOCI214.name: Modern Sociology
GOSSOCI214.finding: Modernity, coloniality, identity and social theories support comparative social interpretation; their documented scope is broader than Nordic societies.

GOSSOCI215.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
GOSSOCI215.finding: The description establishes social movements and environmental justice through feminist, anticolonial and other perspectives. These can frame land/identity issues without establishing Arctic/Sami/Inuit teaching.

GOSSOCI311.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
GOSSOCI311.finding: Civil society, solidarity, trust, public spheres and research on organisations support social-system questions, without a documented Nordic welfare/civil-society sequence.

HCBBIOM111.name: Epidemiology & Public Health
HCBBIOM111.finding: Health determinants, causal study designs, needs assessment and population evidence support social-system comparison; no Nordic health-system case is established.

HCBCOGN312.name: Psycholinguistics
HCBCOGN312.finding: The description substantively teaches language processing, acquisition, bilingualism, semantics, speech, reading and experimental approaches. It is a genuine language-science contribution, but not Scandinavian sociolinguistics or mutual intelligibility.

HCBGATE102.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
HCBGATE102.finding: Brain/behaviour concepts and psychological/neuroscientific methods prepare for psycholinguistics; the remaining clinical/behavioural material cannot be treated as regional cultural study.

MCCCOMM111.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
MCCCOMM111.finding: Rhetorical analysis, argument, discourse and storytelling provide concrete textual/communicative tools, not Scandinavian language competence.

MCCCOMM211.name: Style & Meaning
MCCCOMM211.finding: Stylistics connects grammar, discourse and cognition to literary/nonfiction interpretation. This is substantive linguistic analysis, without a Scandinavian linguistic/source-language sequence.

MCCCOMM311.name: Persuasive Communication
MCCCOMM311.finding: Persuasion, framing and research-based community communication provide applied discourse methods; its sustainability projects do not establish Nordic communication study.

MCCCOMM312.name: Creative Communication Laboratory
MCCCOMM312.finding: Poetry, performance and scholarship-grounded creative practice provide a complementary way to explore language, voice and embodiment, not Nordic source-language or translation training.

MCCHEAM111.name: Introduction to Western Art History
MCCHEAM111.finding: Western painting and contextual visual research support cultural-history interpretation, without evidence of a Nordic art-historical focus.

MCCHEAM211.name: African Art & Heritage
MCCHEAM211.finding: African visual traditions, colonial collecting and restitution provide actual material-culture and heritage inquiry; they are not Scandinavian cultural history.

MCCHEAM316.name: Writing Art's Histories
MCCHEAM316.finding: The description supports art historiography, interpretation, authorship/identity and global disciplinary critique. These methods receive full consideration without invented regional examples.

MCCLITR111.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
MCCLITR111.finding: Close reading, genre, narrative, symbolism and critical-source use directly support literary interpretation as a method; no region-specific corpus is established.

MCCLITR112.name: Great Literary Works
MCCLITR112.finding: Ancient-to-modern literary comparison, historical context and textual analysis support comparative literary history, without a sustained Nordic corpus.

MCCLITR211.name: World Myth & Literature
MCCLITR211.finding: The official description explicitly includes Norse myth within comparative world literature. The profile adds comparative narrative theories and research. This is a genuine regional bridge, but does not establish sustained Scandinavian literary/cultural history.

MCCLITR212.name: Life & Travel Writing
MCCLITR212.finding: Life/travel writing, memory, identity and cultural positioning provide direct methods for narratives of place and belonging; no Nordic travel/memory corpus is established.

MCCLITR311.name: Film & Text
MCCLITR311.finding: Adaptation, intertextuality and close literary/film research support text-image and reception inquiry, without an established Nordic regional focus.

MCCLITR312.name: Perspectives on Literary Meaning
MCCLITR312.finding: The description establishes humanist, feminist, Marxist, minority and psychoanalytic interpretation with a research project. These methods do not themselves provide Scandinavian texts or contexts.

MCCMEDI111.name: Introduction to Film & Media
MCCMEDI111.finding: Film form, history, representation and feminist/postcolonial interpretation provide media-analysis methods, without a Nordic drama/film sequence.

MCCMEDI112.name: Media Archaeology
MCCMEDI112.finding: Media materiality, technologies, communication and memory provide historical-cultural inquiry; Scandinavian urban/digital-language research is not established.

MCCMEDI211.name: From T.V. to TikTok
MCCMEDI211.finding: American media, identity, Indigenous self-representation and speculative futures supply specific cultural comparison, not Nordic popular culture.

MCCMEDI311.name: Media & Race
MCCMEDI311.finding: Racial construction, exclusion, media and observation/archive/podcast methods support identity research; the American setting is not converted into Scandinavian minority history.

MCCMEDI312.name: The Documentary
MCCMEDI312.finding: Documentary theory, interviewing, ethnographic representation and production support qualitative cultural inquiry; no Nordic subject or guaranteed regional project is documented.

candidates.concept: Scandinavian language, linguistics and cultural inquiry
candidates.assessment: The closest trial combines literary interpretation, psycholinguistics, stylistics, rhetoric, creative communication, media, qualitative inquiry and social theory. Psycholinguistics substantively studies language acquisition, processing, bilingualism and experiments; Style and Meaning teaches grammar/discourse/cognition in interpretation. Comparative myth includes Norse material. The combination supports broad language-and-culture inquiry, but does not sustain Scandinavian linguistic relationships, cultural source study or the region’s societies and literatures. Missing language acquisition alone is not the decision criterion.

candidates.concept: Scandinavian literature, cultural history and Nordic identity
candidates.assessment: The second trial tests the complete literature sequence, myth, media/film/documentary, art interpretation, comparative histories, identity theory and qualitative research. These provide substantial methods and cultural-historical inquiry; Norse myth is an actual regional bridge. The history and media courses have their documented American, Indigenous or global settings, and art/heritage study supplies particular non-Nordic settings. Their combined teaching does not accumulate into Scandinavian literary history, northern cultural memory or regional identity research.

candidates.concept: Nordic societies, politics and northern-European history
candidates.assessment: The third trial tests comparative politics, EU institutions and law, international relations, policy, public economics, public health, modern/imperial history, sociology and research methods. Welfare, redistribution, democratic institutions and civil society provide genuine academic responses to interests in social systems. The composition does not establish sustained teaching of Nordic institutions, welfare-model development, regional modern history or the North/Arctic and Indigenous issues that organise the target. The current evidence does not justify carrying forward the old brief-Sweden-example claim as a regional curriculum.

academicChallenge: The strongest language/cultural response combines psycholinguistic experiments, stylistic/discourse analysis, full literary and media interpretation and qualitative/social inquiry, including the actual Norse-myth connection. The second tests cultural memory, historical identities and visual heritage; the third tests institutions, welfare and European society with concrete policy/economic/public-health methods. The alternatives implement those broad concepts but not sustained Nordic regional inquiry. No minimum count of Nordic courses, exact-equivalence rule or requirement that 23 non-PPD courses each teach Scandinavia is imposed. Missing language training alone is insufficient; the regional literature, societies and history shortfall also matters.
progressionAndRepair: Formal prerequisites and actual covered terms were read directly. Brain and Behaviour precedes the only planned Psycholinguistics term, 2027h1. Foundations precede advanced literary, sociological, rhetorical, media and art work where selected. The political trial follows introductory economics and research methods before Public Economics and political foundations before advanced political projects. Initial fall-heavy selections were repaired by comparing coherent spring alternatives, including gender history, ethics and African heritage; no offerings were restored. All three complete trials pass mechanically.
distinctness: Three coherent documented generator groups were tested, not a default required count. Their language/interpretive, historical-cultural and social/institutional priorities lead to different course sets. No programme is accepted, so the approved-alternative distinctness floor is not used to imply approval.
